newsitem.title: LUXEMBOURG: Little Council progress with Swiss transport issue.
newsitem.headline: Little Council progress with Swiss transport issue.

text.p: The Transport Council made little obvious progress on Thursday in its thinking on how to tie up talks on road transport relations with Switzerland.

Transport Commissioner Kinnock began the debate with a warning to transport ministers that without an agreement with Switzerland, member states would be faced with a situation in 2005 -- at the end of the existing transit agreement -- where they would have no control on the new regime devised by Berne.
The Swiss would be free to impose higher charges without having necessarily ceded anything on their current 28-tonne maximum limit on lorry weights, he said.
The talks themselves, part of a package of bilateral issues under discussion since early 1995, aim to allow EU lorries greater access to, and transit through, Switzerland.
The EU has sought immediate access for its trucks to Switzerland's main industrial centres, while Berne wants an access deal to include the right for reciprocal competition in road haulage services.

Linked to access and transit questions is Switzerland's proposal for a phased abolition of its current 28-tonne limit on all lorries, allowing 34-tonne vehicles onto Swiss roads from the start of 2001 and 40 tonners from 2005.

In return Switzerland plans to introduce scaled charges for all lorries on its roads reflecting their infrastructure damage and "nuisance cost" -- a figure based on the amount of noise and pollution caused by the vehicle and associated health effects.

One EU diplomat told reporters that during subsequent discussions the Italian delegation had warned against deciding something which would disadvantage one part of the the EU, namely the Alpine regions, over the rest.

The Austrian delegation, one of the most concerned by the problems of diverted traffic from Swiss routes, said Switzerland should not get any advantages which were not available to EU countries. The point is of particular relevance given Vienna's current legal problems with the Commission over its charging policy for the Brenner pass.

Austrian Transport Minister Rudolf Scholten said 350,000 lorries crossed his country each year because of the current Swiss road transport regime. He said that if these lorries went via Switzerland then in Berne's statistics for transit traffic, the road/rail share of 20/80 would be more like 40/60.

German Transport Minister Matthias Wissmann insisted on four points being at the foundation of any charging system agreed between the two sides. It should be non-discriminatory for Swiss and EU carriers, with no subsidy or aids for Swiss carriers, with the necessary Swiss transit infrastructure in place and with a charging system which had been developed bilaterally.
"After all the interventions, it was not very clear that Kinnock had got what he wanted," the diplomat said.

What Kinnock had sought in a letter to Transport Council President Michael Lowry ahead of the meeting was a clear indication on whether ministers agreed with the principle that by 2005, the bulk of Alpine transit traffic would pay a charge related to the chosen mode's internal and external costs.
Internal costs being those due to operation -- such as fuel, salaries, license and rig costs -- and external ones based on some model of costs to infrastructure, pollution and so on.
A Swiss diplomat said the talks need not rest on the outcome of the EU's internal efforts to set-up its own pricing system for transport systems, as had been widely assumed in recent discussions.
"The destiny of the EU/Swiss agreement has been linked for six months with that of the Euro-vignette it doesn't necessarily need to remain so," the Swiss diplomat told reporters.
He said the beauty of the Swiss proposal was that it largely followed the lines of what the EU it was planning itself and so for the talks to fail would be something of an "own goal" for the bloc.

The transport talks are part of a package of bilateral issues under discussion since early 1995. These include questions such as the elimination of non-tariff trade barriers, air transport liberalisation, scientific research and the free movement of labour.
